extraction.name: CT-RATE
extraction.description: A public open-source dataset pairing non-contrast 3D chest CT volumes with corresponding radiology text reports. The dataset comprises 25,692 scans from 21,304 unique patients and 50,188 reconstructed 3D chest CT volumes, with each exam accompanied by a report including findings and impression sections. The dataset is used to develop CT-CLIP and CT-CHAT.
extraction.creator: Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci
extraction.citeAs: Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci. CT-RATE: Paired chest CT volumes and radiology reports. https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibrahimhamamci/CT-RATE. 2025.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was curated from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital and consists of non-contrast chest CT volumes and corresponding radiology text reports. It includes 50,188 reconstructed CT volumes from 25,692 distinct CT experiments conducted on 21,304 unique patients. Every reconstructed volume from the hospital database was incorporated to capture different reconstruction techniques used for specific diagnostic requirements. Reports were anonymized, translated from Turkish to English using the Google Translate API, and reviewed and corrected by bilingual final-year medical students. CT volumes were quality controlled to exclude contrast-enhanced scans and scans involving body parts other than the chest, and metadata were anonymized.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consist of chest CT volumes, associated metadata, and radiology text reports from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital hospital records/database. The CT-RATE dataset contains the original raw data.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Reports were anonymized by removing personal information pertaining to patients and medical professionals using targeted searches with regular expressions to identify and eliminate date-related information and patient-doctor identifiers. Reports were then translated from Turkish to English using the Google Translate API and reviewed and corrected by bilingual final-year medical students, who also removed any residual personal information and ensured coherence. Similar abnormality conditions were grouped during report annotation, such as left and right mucoid impactions under mucoid impaction, various lung opacities under lung opacity, and lung and fissural nodules under lung nodules.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Volumes involving contrast material or body parts other than the chest were excluded. Each chest CT volume's orientation was standardized by examining metadata. Each volume was resized to uniform spacing of 0.75 mm in x and y and 1.5 mm in z, then center-cropped or padded to a consistent resolution of 480×480×240. CT volumes were converted to Hounsfield Unit values using intercept and slope values from metadata, clipped to the range -1000 to 1000, and normalized to -1 to 1 during training. Identifying information was removed from metadata.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each volume is annotated with 18 abnormalities for validation and fine-tuning. To develop an automated label extractor model, 1,000 reports were manually annotated by merging findings and impression sections into a multi-label dataset covering 18 abnormalities. Conditions not referenced in either section were considered absent. The annotated reports were split into training (800) and validation (200) sets. A pretrained language model, RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m, was finetuned on these annotations and then applied to classify the remaining 24,692 reports. In addition, organ-level anatomical segmentation labels were generated using a state-of-the-art segmentation model and made openly available.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The findings and impression sections were merged because some abnormalities are not explicitly mentioned in a single section. The finetuned report classifier's precision, recall, and F1 scores are reported in Supplementary Table 2 and described as showing robust classification across abnormalities, ensuring high-quality labels. Conditions not referenced in either section were considered absent.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 1,000 reports were manually annotated once each for 18 abnormalities; three board-certified radiologists independently rated 150 generated reports per model for expert evaluation
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Bilingual final-year medical students reviewed and corrected report translations and examined reports for residual personal information; three board-certified radiologists independently rated generated reports; two board-certified thoracic radiologists were from Zurich and one radiologist was from Istanbul
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Google Translate API, RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m, automated report labeler, TotalSegmentator, state-of-the-art segmentation model
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is publicly accessible via Hugging Face, and trained models and codebases are publicly available on GitHub. The paper states plans to extend CT-RATE with multi-abnormality segmentation and localization labels for 3D chest CT volumes as future work, and notes open-source release of organ-level anatomical segmentation labels through the CT-RATE repository on Hugging Face.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Patient age, sex, clinical information, medical history, symptoms, scan metadata, and radiology reports originally containing personal information. The study states that all chest CT volumes, associated metadata, and radiology text reports were anonymized before computational analysis.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that CT-RATE, CT-CLIP, and CT-CHAT address critical challenges in 3D medical imaging, lay groundwork for future innovations in medical AI, and may improve patient care. The models are described as potentially reducing radiologists' workload, enhancing workflows, saving time and effort, improving diagnostic accuracy, and broadening accessibility through a user-friendly graphical interface for educational and clinical research settings.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper explicitly states that biases inherent to the single-institution dataset may influence self-supervised training. Although the dataset is large and diverse, the data originate from a single geographic and clinical setting, which may limit generalizability to other populations. The paper also notes that CT-CLIP depends on the specific terminology used in reports and the choice of prompts during zero-shot detection, and that variability in how diseases are described across radiology reports can affect detection accuracy.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset and models have several stated limitations: the dataset is from a single institution and single geographic and clinical setting, which may limit generalizability; CT-CLIP depends on report terminology and prompt choice; evaluation of CT-CHAT is limited by the lack of pretrained 3D medical multimodal AI assistants for benchmarking, so comparisons are made against 2D models using DRRs; the quality of CT-CHAT generated reports remains insufficient for clinical use; the models are currently limited to chest CT volumes; and substantial challenges such as robustness, interpretability, regulatory compliance, and prospective validation remain before clinical deployment.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is used for training and internal validation of CT-CLIP and CT-CHAT, for fine-tuning, for zero-shot multi-abnormality detection, for supervised baseline training, for volume-to-volume and report-to-volume retrieval, for report generation, and for creation of a visual question-answering dataset. The cohort was split into training and validation groups, with 20,000 patients allocated to training and 1,304 to validation. The paper emphasizes research use and benchmarking, and explicitly states that current models and generated reports are not ready for clinical deployment or routine clinical use.
